abstract: Most documented examples of plant adaptive radiations occur on oceanic islands, but high-elevation mountain systems offer similar ecological opportunities. Here, we investigate the genus Puya (Bromeliaceae), a rapidly diversifying Andean lineage associated with high-elevation ecosystems, to assess how ecological opportunity and biotic interactions shape diversification and morphological evolution in fragmented mountain landscapes. Using a phylogenomic dataset for the Septentrional Clade of Puya, a clade largely restricted to the paramo habitat, we performed biogeographic reconstructions and trait evolution analyses using parametric models. We identified a temporal increase in diversification rates consistent with the onset of paramo expansion, together with a clade-specific increase in lineages associated with this ecosystem. Likewise, we found that character displacement and competitive exclusion drove phenotypic divergence and identified signatures of pulsed evolution. We propose the Septentrional Clade of Puya as a new example of adaptive radiation in continental sky-island systems and demonstrate that ecological opportunity and biotic interactions jointly shaped its evolutionary history. Our findings provide new insights into how ecological pressures shape macroevolutionary patterns in highly diverse plant clades and show that mountain radiations can generate morphological diversity through processes comparable to those documented in classic examples of adaptive radiations in oceanic islands.
